actions.name: Aggregate
actions.help: Groups rows with equal values in the group columns and calculates one result row per group, like GROUP BY in SQL. Groups appear in the order they first occur. A sum of only empty values is empty, as in SQL (and in Pivot), also for a table without rows.

actions.name: Calculate columns
actions.help:
Adds columns calculated with SQL-style formulas. A column from an earlier step with the same name is replaced; the new columns of one step need different names. Each formula can use the columns calculated above it.

Examples: [Price] * [Quantity] · ROUND([Net] * 1.19, 2) · UPPER(TRIM([Name])) · [First name] || ' ' || [Last name] · IIF([Amount] > 1000, 'big', 'small') · CASE WHEN [Country] = 'DE' THEN 'Germany' ELSE 'Other' END · YEAR([Date]) · [Date] + 30 (days) · SUM([Amount]) OVER (PARTITION BY [Customer])

actions.name: Number rows
actions.help:
Adds a running number.

Number the rows: 1, 2, 3, … over the whole table, or restarting for each group (like ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY … ORDER BY …) in SQL). Number the groups: every distinct combination of the group columns gets its own number (like DENSE_RANK()). The order of the rows in the table does not change.

options.label: Number the groups: equal values get the same number

settings.label: In this order (empty = current row order)

actions.name: Check data
actions.help:
Checks the data at this step: when a check fails, it stops the table or only warns. The data itself stays as it is.

Number of rows: at least, at most, exactly or between two numbers; at least 1 means that the table must not be empty. Stop the table: the step shows an error, like a step that fails, so the steps after it and the tables that use this table are not calculated and their exports don't run; a run of the project fails. Only warn: the step and Run results show a warning, and the data goes on. Put the step before the exports, so that bad input never overwrites a good file.

settings.label: When a check fails
settings.help: Stop the table: the step shows an error, the steps after it and the tables that use this table are not calculated, and a run of the project fails. Only warn: the step shows a warning and the data goes on.

actions.name: Change type / format
actions.help:
Converts columns to another type.

Format examples — dates: dd.mm.yyyy, yyyy-mm-dd, dd.mm.yyyy hh:mm, d. mmmm yyyy; numbers as text: 0.00, #,##0.00, 00000 (pads with zeros, e.g. postal codes), 0%, #,##0.00 €. Without a date format, common formats are detected; two-digit years are read like in Excel (25 = 2025, 75 = 1975). Month and day names (mmm, mmmm, ddd, dddd) are English. Numbers become dates as Excel day numbers (45658 = 01.01.2025); with a format of digits only, such as yyyymmdd, their digits are read with it (20260131 = 31.01.2026). Whole numbers keep all their digits (up to 9,223,372,036,854,775,807); decimal numbers keep about 15.

actions.name: Rename columns
actions.help: Gives columns new names.

actions.name: Keep, remove or reorder columns
actions.help: Keeps only some columns (in the order listed), removes columns, or moves columns to the front while keeping all others behind them.

options.label: Keep only these columns, in this order
Move these columns to the front

actions.name: Export to CSV / text file
actions.help:
Writes the table to a delimited text file. An existing file is replaced when the new one is complete: if the export fails, the old file stays as it was.

Decimal numbers are written with at most 15 significant digits, as Excel shows and saves them: 0.37 * 3 is 1,11 (not 1,1099999999999999). Whole numbers and exact decimals keep all their digits. Times keep their fractions of a second (08:30:00.500). Binary values are written as hex text (0x0102FF), time spans as text that is the same on every PC (1d 2h 3m, as Pivot and Split column write them); infinite and not-a-number values as empty, as in Excel. A table without columns gives an empty file. A CSV file can't hold lists or records: such columns stop the export.

settings.label: Don't export an empty table
settings.help: When the table has no rows, the file is left as it is.

options.label: UTF-8 with BOM (Excel opens it correctly)

actions.name: Import CSV / text files
actions.help:
Reads a delimited text file (CSV, TXT, TSV), or all such files of a folder (and its subfolders) into one table: daily exports, for example.

Delimiter, encoding and decimal separator are detected automatically unless chosen; a file whose first line has no delimiter has one column. Numbers and dates are recognized when every value of a column fits: also amounts like 1.234,50 €, -$3.00 or 123,45- and percentages like 12,5% (read as 0.125). Numbers keep all their digits: whole numbers of up to 19 digits are integers, longer ones and decimals that a decimal number would round (12345678901234,5678) exact decimals (up to 38 digits; longer ones stay text, with a warning). Columns with leading zeros (customer numbers, postal codes, 00,5) stay text, and so do digits with spaces between them (phone numbers, card numbers): spaces between thousands count only in amounts and percentages (1 234,50 €). A value like 1.000 can be one thousand or one: it follows the other numbers of its column (like 0.500 or 2,5, also in the other files of a folder), else those of its file, and without any it is one thousand in files with semicolons.

In a folder, each file is read with its own delimiter, encoding, decimal separator and date format. Files are matched by column names; a column missing in a file stays empty there. A column with other types in other files gets a type that holds every value, as in Append, or becomes text with a warning; one that is text in a file stays text, as the files have it.

settings.label: File names
settings.help: * stands for any text, e.g. orders_*.csv; several patterns with ;

settings.label: When there are no files
settings.help: e.g. for a folder that is empty on some days: skipping leaves out the steps after this one. An empty table (with a warning) has only the columns with the file name and the path, as far as they are switched on below: a later step that names another column fails.

options.label: Skip the rest of the table

settings.label: Add a column with the file name
Add a column with the path below the folder

settings.label: First row has the column names

settings.help: Off: every column stays text.

actions.name: Run SQL command
actions.help: Runs SQL in a database, e.g. a stored procedure after an export, or DELETE / UPDATE statements. SQL Server: separate batches with GO lines, as in SSMS (GO 3 runs a batch three times). Runs only when the project is run, in one transaction: if it fails, its changes are rolled back. SQLite refuses BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK; on SQL Server, a BEGIN TRAN … COMMIT of the command's own works, and a COMMIT or ROLLBACK that ends the transaction of the step stops it with a message. Stop ends a statement that runs. The table passes through unchanged.

settings.label: SQL
settings.help: The database's own SQL (T-SQL for SQL Server)

actions.name: Export to database
actions.help:
Writes the table into a database table, in one transaction: if anything fails, the database stays as it was.

Add the rows, replace all of them, or replace just the rows with the same key values (e.g. the dates in the data: reloading a day replaces that day). Update rows by key columns, or update them and add the new ones. Columns are matched by name; a missing table is created with types that fit the data. Values are stored as their columns hold them, the same way in every mode (08:00:01.5 is 08:00:01 in a SQL Server datetime2(0) column, and the step says how many values were cut; spaces at the end of a text that don't fit are left out), and key values compare as their columns do (e.g. with their collation). On SQL Server, a text for a date or time column is read as Change type / format reads it without a format (31.12.2025 08:30, 2025-12-31): a text it can't read stops the export. Date-times with a time zone are written in that zone's local time, without the zone (08:30 in Berlin stays 08:30), as in the Excel export; into a SQL Server datetimeoffset column with the zone's offset (08:30 +02:00), and there a date-time without a zone gets the offset of this PC's time zone on its day. Binary values for a SQL Server column of text are hex text (0x0102FF), as the CSV export writes them. Runs only when the project is run.

Delete the rows where a condition is true, then add
Update the rows with the same key values

Delete the rows with the same key values

settings.help: The columns that identify a row, e.g. OrderNo, or Date to replace whole days

settings.label: Delete the rows where
settings.help: A condition in the database's own SQL (T-SQL for SQL Server)

Don't export an empty table

actions.name: Import from database
actions.help: Reads a whole table or view, or the result of a SQL query written in the database's own SQL dialect (T-SQL for SQL Server). Imports also run while editing, e.g. when a project is opened, so they change nothing: a SQLite file is opened for reading only, and what a query changes in SQL Server is rolled back (a query that commits by itself keeps its changes). Numbers keep all their digits: a column with numbers of more digits than a decimal number keeps (about 15), or with whole numbers too big for a whole-number column, stays a column of exact decimals. A SQL Server datetimeoffset column becomes date-times in UTC, the moments it holds, or (as steps saved before this choice read it) text with its offset, 2026-10-01T08:30:00+02:00; SQL Server's driver reads date-times to the microsecond, and for a column with 7 digits of a second the step says that a 7th digit, if any, is cut. "Detect numbers and dates in text columns" finds them in text, with the decimal separator of each column as the CSV import does (also in amounts and percentages), or only numbers and dates with a chosen one; steps saved before it could be chosen use the point, as they did.

settings.label: Detect numbers and dates in text columns
Decimal separator
settings.help: Detect automatically: each column's own, as the CSV import detects it, also in amounts (1.234,50 €) and percentages (12,5%). Point or Comma: numbers and dates with that separator, no amounts or percentages.

settings.label: SQL Server datetimeoffset columns
settings.help: Only for SQL Server. Date-times in UTC: the moments the column holds (2026-10-01 08:30 +02:00 is 06:30). Text with the offset: as written, 2026-10-01T08:30:00+02:00; steps saved before this choice read them so.

actions.name: Export to Excel file
actions.help:
Writes the table to an .xlsx file, as an Excel table with formats. An existing file is replaced, or only the sheet is: in a workbook with reports, charts and pivot tables built on the sheet, also in one with macros (.xlsm). The Excel table keeps its name; charts, named ranges and pivot tables that covered the old rows cover the new rows. The file is replaced when the new one is complete: if the export fails, the old file stays as it was.

Formats use Excel's codes: #,##0.00 for numbers with thousands separators, 0% for percentages, dd.mm.yyyy for dates. Excel shows them in your regional style. Binary values are written as hex text (0x0102FF). A sheet holds up to 1,048,575 rows below its header and 32,767 characters in a cell. Column names must differ in more than upper and lower case: an Excel table can't tell Name and NAME apart, so the export stops.

Text stays text, exactly as it is: =1+1 is no formula, and a web address is no clickable link in the file.

settings.label: If the file exists
settings.help: Replace the whole file: a new workbook with only this sheet. Replace only this sheet: everything else in the workbook stays as it is (the other sheets with their formulas, formatting, charts, pivot tables and macros) and shows the new data when Excel opens the file.

options.label: Replace only this sheet, keep the other sheets

settings.label: Fit column widths to the content

actions.help:
Reads Excel files (xlsx, xlsm, xlsb, xls) or OpenDocument spreadsheets: one file or all files of a folder (and its subfolders), one sheet, all sheets or the sheets whose names match, into one table.

Rows above the header row are skipped. Excel stores every number as a decimal number; columns that only hold whole numbers become integers, cells with only a time become times. Sheets and files are matched by column names; a column missing in one stays empty there.

Merged cells keep their value in the first cell only: 'Fill empty values' fills the others. Formulas give the results Excel saved with the file; a file written by another program may have none (the column stays empty): open it in Excel and save it.

actions.name: Import Parquet files
actions.help: Reads a Parquet file, or all Parquet files of a folder (and its subfolders) into one table. Parquet is the compact, column-based format of data lakes (written by Spark, Databricks, pandas, DuckDB, ...); column types are stored in the file, so nothing has to be detected. Decimal columns keep all their digits: those without decimal places become whole numbers when every value fits, the others stay exact decimals; numbers of more than 38 digits become text. Whole numbers of 128 bits follow the same rules. Files are matched by column names.

actions.name: Pivot
actions.help:
Turns the values of one column into columns, like an Excel pivot table without totals: one row for each combination of the row keys, one column for each value, and in each cell the values of the rows that meet there, added up (or counted, averaged, …).

The new columns are named after the values: text as it is, numbers as 1234 or 1.5, dates as 2025-12-31, true/false as true and false; empty values go into one column (empty). They are sorted, or come in the order they first appear; a name that exists already gets " (2)", or the next number that isn't the name of another value. Rows come in the order their keys first appear. A cell without rows stays empty, and so does a sum of only empty values. Count counts the values that are not empty; First and Last take the first and last value that is not empty (text with nothing but spaces counts here, as in Aggregate). At most 1,000 new columns, and at most 50,000,000 cells (rows × new columns).

settings.label: Row keys (empty = one total row)
settings.help: One row for each combination of their values, in the order they first appear.

settings.label: Column names from
settings.help: Each value of this column becomes a new column.

settings.label: Values from
settings.help: The values that fill the new columns.

settings.label: Function
settings.help: How the values of the rows that meet in one cell are combined.

actions.name: Unpivot
actions.help:
Turns columns into rows, the opposite of Pivot: each row becomes one row for each chosen column, with the column's name in a new name column and its value in a new value column; the other columns are repeated. Example: Customer, Jan, Feb, Mar becomes Customer, Month, Amount with three rows per customer.

The rows keep their order, and the values of a row come in the order of the columns. Columns of one type keep it. Whole and decimal numbers become decimal numbers, whole numbers and exact decimals exact decimals, dates and date-times date-times, when every value stays as it is (whole numbers beyond 9,223,372,036,854,775,807 become exact decimals). Any other mix, also decimal numbers with exact decimals, becomes text (numbers as 1.5, exact decimals as 2.00, dates as 2025-12-31), and the step says so. A column whose values are all empty doesn't count, whatever its type. At most 250,000,000 cells in the result (rows × columns).

settings.label: New column for the names
settings.help: Holds the name of the column each value comes from.

settings.label: Leave out empty values
settings.help: Off: each row gives one row for every column, also for an empty cell.

actions.name: Remove duplicates
actions.help: Removes rows that are equal in the compared columns. The row order is kept.

settings.label: Of rows that are equal, keep

actions.name: Fill empty values
actions.help: Fills empty cells: with the value above (typical for Excel lists where a group name is only written once), the value below, or a fixed value. Empty text counts as empty.

actions.name: Filter rows
actions.help:
Keeps (or removes) the rows that match the conditions.

Values are compared with the column's type: numbers as numbers (1,5 or 1.5), dates as dates (31.12.2025, 2025-12-31 or "today"), times as times (08:30 or 08:30:15). Empty cells never equal a value, but they count as "does not equal" and "does not contain".

options.label: is greater than or equal to
is less than or equal to

actions.name: Filter rows by formula
actions.help: Keeps (or removes) the rows for which a SQL-style condition is true, e.g. [Amount] > 100 AND [Country] IN ('DE', 'AT') or [Date] >= DATE '2025-01-01'.

actions.name: Sort
actions.help: Sorts the rows. Text is sorted like in Excel: upper and lower case count the same, letters with accents sort with their base letter (ä with a), ß like ss. Rows with equal values keep their order.

actions.name: Append other tables
actions.help: Adds the rows of other tables below the rows of this table. Columns are matched by name. A column with different types in the tables gets the type that Unpivot gives its value column: whole and decimal numbers become decimal numbers, whole numbers and exact decimals exact decimals, dates and date-times date-times, when every value stays as it is. Any other mix becomes text, and the step says so. A table in which the column has only empty values doesn't count. Lists and records can't be in one column with values of another type.

settings.label: Tables to append below this one

options.label: All columns of all tables (missing values stay empty)
Only the columns of this table

actions.name: Start from another table
actions.help: Starts this table with the result of another table, so you can branch off and transform it differently without touching the original.

actions.name: Merge with another table
actions.help:
Combines this table with another table by matching key columns.

Lookup (the default, like a lookup in a spreadsheet) adds columns from the first matching row, so the row count never changes. Left, inner and full join work like in SQL: every matching row is used, so a row repeats when the other table has several matches. Keep rows with or without a match filters this table without adding columns. The step tells how many rows matched and shows a few keys of the rows without a match. Empty keys never match. Whole numbers and exact decimals are compared with all their digits, also when their types differ. Keys of different types (a number and a text) are compared as text, the same on every PC (the decimal number 17.0 finds the text 17); the key columns keep their type, except in a full join whose other table has keys that don't fit it (2.5 for whole numbers): then they get a type that fits both. Lists and records match only keys of their own type.

fields.label: equals column in the other table

Inner join (only rows with a match)
Full join (all rows of both tables)

settings.label: If several rows of the other table match

actions.name: Clean text
actions.help: Tidies up text: removes surrounding or repeated spaces and line breaks, changes upper/lower case, pads values to a fixed length (e.g. postal codes 1234 → 01234). Selected columns that are not text are turned into text, the same on every PC: 17 (not 17.0), 2025-12-31 08:30:00.

settings.label: Replace line breaks with a space
Pad to length (0 = off)
settings.help: Adds characters at the start, e.g. 1234 → 01234

settings.label: Make empty text an empty value

actions.name: Replace
actions.help:
Replaces values.

Whole cell value: cells equal to "Find" get the new value; an empty "Find" matches empty cells, an empty "Replace with" makes cells empty. Text inside: every occurrence is replaced. Regular expression: "Replace with" can use $1, $2, ... for groups ($1_$2 is group 1, _ and group 2), ${name} for a named group and $$ for a $ sign; a backslash is a normal character (\1 is the text \1, with a warning that group 1 is written $1).

actions.name: Split column
actions.help:
Splits the text of a column at a separator, into columns or into rows.

Into columns: "Müller, Hans" becomes Müller and Hans in two new columns, which take the place of the column. There are as many parts as new columns: the last one gets the rest of the text ("Müller, Hans, Dr." gives Müller and Hans, Dr.), and missing parts stay empty. Into rows: "A;B;C" becomes three rows, with the other columns repeated; empty parts are left out, and a row without any part stays, with an empty value.

The parts are text; a part with nothing but spaces is empty. With Space, several spaces in a row are one separator. A column that is not text is turned into text first: 2.5 and 2 (not 2.0), exact decimals with their decimal places (2.00), 2026-02-27, 2026-02-27 08:30:00 (fractions of a second only when there are some).

options.label: Columns: one new column per part

settings.label: Separator text
settings.help: Any text, e.g. / or - (as it is, not a pattern).

settings.label: New columns (one per part)
settings.help: The last one gets the rest of the text. Without a name: Name 1, Name 2, … after the column.

functions.name: ILIKE
functions.summary: Like LIKE, but upper and lower case don't matter
Joins texts (+ only adds numbers)
functions.note: When one of the values is empty, the result is empty; CONCAT skips empty values.

functions.syntax: a + b, a - b, a * b, a / b
functions.summary: Add, subtract, multiply, divide
Whole-number division of whole numbers: 7 // 2 = 3
functions.note: It rounds toward zero: -7 // 2 = -3. For decimal numbers // divides normally (7.5 // 2 = 3.75): use FLOOR(a / b) or TRUNC(a / b) there.

functions.summary: The remainder of a division: 7 % 2 = 1

functions.name: UPPER
functions.summary: The text in uppercase (ß becomes SS)
functions.note: A capital first letter only (like PROPER for one word): UPPER(LEFT([Name], 1)) || LOWER(SUBSTRING([Name], 2)).

functions.name: LOWER
functions.summary: The text in lowercase

functions.name: TRIM
functions.summary: Removes spaces (or the given characters) from both ends

functions.name: LTRIM
functions.summary: Removes spaces (or the given characters) from the start

functions.name: RTRIM
functions.summary: Removes spaces (or the given characters) from the end

functions.name: LEN
functions.summary: The number of characters; spaces at the end don't count (as in SQL Server)

functions.name: LENGTH
functions.summary: The number of characters, all spaces counted

functions.name: LEFT
functions.summary: The first count characters

functions.name: RIGHT
functions.summary: The last count characters

functions.name: SUBSTRING
functions.summary: Part of the text; start 1 is the first character

functions.name: REPLACE
functions.summary: Replaces every occurrence of find (case-sensitive)

functions.name: CONCAT
functions.summary: Joins the values; empty values are skipped

functions.name: CONCAT_WS
functions.summary: Joins the values with a separator; empty values are skipped

functions.name: CHARINDEX
functions.summary: Where find is in the text (1 = first character), 0 if it isn't; case-sensitive
functions.note: Unlike SQL Server's usual setting, upper and lower case matter: CHARINDEX(LOWER('B'), LOWER([Code])) ignores them.

functions.name: INSTR
functions.summary: Where find is in the text (1 = first character), 0 if it isn't; case-sensitive

functions.name: CONTAINS
functions.summary: True when the text contains find (case-sensitive)

functions.name: STARTS_WITH
functions.summary: True when the text starts with the given text (case-sensitive)

functions.name: ENDS_WITH
functions.summary: True when the text ends with the given text (case-sensitive)

functions.name: LPAD
functions.summary: Fills up on the left to the length, e.g. with leading zeros
functions.note: A longer text is cut to the length: LPAD('1234567', 3, '0') gives '123'. Numbers need CAST(... AS VARCHAR) first.

functions.name: RPAD
functions.summary: Fills up on the right to the length
functions.note: A longer text is cut to the length.

functions.name: SPLIT_PART
functions.summary: The n-th part of the text, split at the separator; -1 is the last part
functions.note: A part that doesn't exist gives an empty text ('').

functions.name: REPEAT
functions.summary: The text repeated count times

functions.name: REVERSE
functions.summary: The characters in reverse order

functions.name: TRANSLATE
functions.summary: Replaces single characters: the n-th of from by the n-th of to

functions.name: STRIP_ACCENTS
functions.summary: Removes accents and umlaut dots: 'Müller Ångström' gives 'Muller Angstrom'

functions.name: REGEXP_MATCHES
functions.summary: True when the regular expression matches somewhere in the text

functions.name: REGEXP_EXTRACT
functions.summary: The part that matches the regular expression (or one group), '' if none

functions.name: REGEXP_REPLACE
functions.summary: Replaces the first match ('g': every match)

functions.name: FORMAT
functions.summary: Fills the {} in the template: {:.2f} two decimals, {:,} thousands separators
functions.note: {:.2f} needs a decimal number: for whole numbers write [Amount] * 1.0. When a value is empty, the result is empty.

functions.name: CHR
functions.summary: The character with this code; CHR(10) is a line break

functions.name: LEVENSHTEIN
functions.summary: How many characters must change to turn one text into the other
functions.note: Useful to find similar spellings.

functions.name: JARO_WINKLER_SIMILARITY
functions.summary: How similar two texts are, from 0 (not at all) to 1 (equal)

functions.name: MD5
functions.summary: A 32-character code calculated from the text, e.g. as a key

functions.name: GEN_RANDOM_UUID
functions.summary: A new random ID (UUID) for every row

functions.name: ROUND
functions.summary: Rounds to the given number of decimals (halves away from zero)
functions.note: Decimal numbers are stored in binary, so a few halves such as 1.005 round down. For exact results round a DECIMAL: ROUND(CAST([Price] AS DECIMAL(18,3)), 2).

functions.name: CEIL
functions.summary: Rounds up to a whole number
functions.note: The result stays a decimal number (3.0); CAST(CEIL([Price]) AS BIGINT) gives an integer.

functions.name: FLOOR
functions.summary: Rounds down to a whole number
functions.note: The result stays a decimal number (3.0); CAST(FLOOR([Price]) AS BIGINT) gives an integer.

functions.name: TRUNC
functions.summary: Cuts off the decimals (or keeps the given number of them)
functions.note: The result stays a decimal number (3.0); CAST(TRUNC([Price]) AS BIGINT) gives an integer.

functions.name: ABS
functions.summary: The number without its sign

functions.name: SIGN
functions.summary: The sign of the number: -1, 0 or 1

functions.name: MOD
functions.summary: The remainder of a division (the same as number % divisor)

functions.name: POWER
functions.summary: The number to the power of the exponent (also number ** exponent)

functions.name: SQRT
functions.summary: The square root

functions.name: EXP
functions.summary: e to the power of the number

functions.name: LN
functions.summary: The natural logarithm

functions.name: LOG
functions.summary: The logarithm to base 10 (or to the given base)

functions.name: RANDOM
functions.summary: A random number between 0 and 1, new for every row and calculation

functions.name: PI
functions.summary: The number π (3.14159…)

functions.name: GETDATE
functions.summary: The current date and time (as in SQL Server)

functions.name: TODAY
functions.summary: The current date (also CURRENT_DATE)
functions.note: For a date column, TODAY() - [Date] gives the days since the date; for date-times use DATE_DIFF('day', [Time], GETDATE()).

functions.name: YEAR
functions.summary: The year

functions.name: QUARTER
functions.summary: The quarter, 1 to 4

functions.name: MONTH
functions.summary: The month, 1 to 12

functions.name: WEEK
functions.summary: The ISO week number, 1 to 53
functions.note: Days around New Year can belong to week 1 of the next year or week 53 of the previous one: use ISOYEAR([Date]) with it (YEARWEEK([Date]) gives 202501).

functions.name: ISOYEAR
functions.summary: The year that the ISO week belongs to (for 30 Dec 2024: 2025)

functions.name: DAY
functions.summary: The day of the month, 1 to 31

functions.name: DAYOFYEAR
functions.summary: The day of the year, 1 to 366

functions.name: ISODOW
functions.summary: The weekday: 1 = Monday ... 7 = Sunday

functions.name: DAYNAME
functions.summary: The English name of the weekday

functions.name: MONTHNAME
functions.summary: The English name of the month

functions.name: HOUR
functions.summary: The hour, 0 to 23

functions.name: MINUTE
functions.summary: The minute, 0 to 59

functions.name: SECOND
functions.summary: The second, 0 to 59

functions.name: DATE_TRUNC
functions.summary: The start of the year, quarter, month, week or day
functions.note: The result is a date-time; add ::DATE for a date.

functions.name: DATE_PART
functions.summary: One part of a date, e.g. year, month, day, week, isodow, doy or hour
functions.note: The part is written in quotes, as the first argument.

functions.name: DATE_DIFF
functions.summary: How many day, month, year (...) boundaries lie between two dates
functions.note: It counts the boundaries crossed, as DATEDIFF in SQL Server: 31 January to 1 February is 1 month, 31 December to 1 January is 1 year. For complete months or years, e.g. an age, use DATE_SUB. The part is written in quotes: 'day', 'month', 'year', 'hour', 'minute'.

functions.name: DATE_SUB
functions.summary: How many complete days, months or years (...) lie between two dates
functions.note: 31 January to 1 February is 0 months. DATE_SUB('year', [Birthday], TODAY()) gives the age.

functions.name: + INTERVAL
functions.summary: The date plus days, months or years
functions.note: The result is a date-time; add ::DATE for a date. With a column write INTERVAL ([Months]) MONTH, or [Date] + TO_MONTHS([Months]). [Date] + 30 adds 30 days and stays a date.

functions.name: LAST_DAY
functions.summary: The last day of the month

functions.name: MAKE_DATE
functions.summary: A date from its parts

functions.name: STRFTIME
functions.summary: The date as text, e.g. %d.%m.%Y, %Y-%m, %B (month name) or %H:%M

functions.name: STRPTIME
functions.summary: Reads a date-time from text in the given format; an error if it doesn't fit
functions.note: The result is a date-time; add ::DATE for a date.

functions.name: TRY_STRPTIME
functions.summary: Like STRPTIME, but empty when the text doesn't fit
functions.note: The result is a date-time; add ::DATE for a date.

functions.name: CAST
functions.summary: Converts to VARCHAR (text), BIGINT (whole number), DOUBLE (decimal number), DECIMAL(18,2), DATE, TIMESTAMP (date-time) or BOOLEAN (true/false)
functions.note: BIGINT rounds to the nearest whole number (halves to the even one): use TRUNC or FLOOR first to cut off. Text must be written 2025-12-31 and 1.5: use STRPTIME for other date formats and REPLACE([Text], ',', '.') for a decimal comma.

functions.name: TRY_CAST
functions.summary: Like CAST, but empty instead of an error when it can't be converted
functions.note: TRY_CAST([Value] AS DOUBLE) IS NOT NULL tells whether a text is a number.

functions.summary: The short form of CAST

functions.name: DATE '...'
functions.summary: A fixed date (also TIMESTAMP '2025-12-31 23:59')

functions.name: SUM ... OVER
functions.summary: The total of the row's group on every row (OVER (): the whole table)
functions.note: AVG, MIN, MAX and COUNT work the same way.

functions.name: COUNT(*) ... OVER
functions.summary: The number of rows in the row's group

functions.name: Running total
functions.summary: The running total in the given order (per group with PARTITION BY)
functions.note: Rows with the same value in the ORDER BY column get the same total; add a second column to ORDER BY, or ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING, to add them one by one.

functions.name: Moving average
functions.syntax: AVG(value) OVER (ORDER BY column ROWS BETWEEN n PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
functions.summary: The average of the row and the n rows before it, in the given order (with SUM: the moving sum)
functions.note: The first rows have fewer rows before them: theirs is the average of the rows there are. Empty values don't count. For each customer apart, write PARTITION BY [Customer] before ORDER BY.
functions.example: AVG([Amount]) OVER (ORDER BY [Date] ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)

functions.name: STDDEV_SAMP ... OVER
functions.summary: The standard deviation of the values: of the whole column with OVER (), of the last rows with ROWS BETWEEN
functions.note: Of the row and the 2 rows before it: STDDEV_SAMP([Amount]) OVER (ORDER BY [Date] ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW). It is the standard deviation of a sample, as Excel's STDEV.S; STDDEV_POP is the one of a whole population (STDEV.P). Empty values don't count; with fewer than 2 values the result is empty.

functions.name: Change in %
functions.syntax: 100.0 * (value - LAG(value) OVER (ORDER BY ...)) / NULLIF(LAG(value) OVER (ORDER BY ...), 0)
functions.summary: The change from the row before, in percent: 25 for 80 after 64
functions.note: The first row has no row before it: its change is empty, and so is the change of an empty value and of the value after one. After a 0 the change is empty too (NULLIF): dividing by 0 would give ∞. For each customer apart, write PARTITION BY [Customer] in both OVER (...). Without 100.0 * the change is a fraction (0.25), for the Excel format 0%.
functions.example: 100.0 * ([Amount] - LAG([Amount]) OVER (ORDER BY [Date])) / NULLIF(LAG([Amount]) OVER (ORDER BY [Date]), 0)

functions.name: ROW_NUMBER
functions.summary: Numbers the rows 1, 2, 3 ... within each group

functions.name: RANK
functions.summary: The rank; equal values share a rank, then numbers are skipped

functions.name: DENSE_RANK
functions.summary: The rank without gaps after equal values

functions.name: LAG
functions.summary: The value of the previous row (or rows back)

functions.name: LEAD
functions.summary: The value of the next row (or rows ahead)

functions.name: FIRST_VALUE
functions.summary: The first value in the row's group

functions.name: LAST_VALUE
functions.syntax: LAST_VALUE(value) OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... ROWS BETWEEN ...)
functions.summary: The last value in the row's group
functions.note: Without ROWS BETWEEN ..., the window ends at the current row (and rows with the same order value).
functions.example: LAST_VALUE([Amount]) OVER (PARTITION BY [Customer] ORDER BY [Date] ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING)

functions.name: NTILE
functions.summary: Splits the rows into n groups of nearly equal size: 1 ... n

functions.name: STRING_AGG ... OVER
functions.summary: All texts of the row's group, joined
